This experimental project, funded by the [Leverhulme Trust](https://www.leverhulme.ac.uk/), is a collaboration between artists and humanists (composition, literary studies, musicology), scientists (biology, psychology, animal cognition), and a research software engineer, who came together to explore historical and contemporary approaches to the study of bee 'sentience', and create a digital bee book that could contain our different research findings. Here we introduce our [digital bee book]({base}/) (our research 'hive'), and our [born-digital edition]({base}/literature/transcription) of the seventeenth-century printed book that inspired it. You can find out more about why we chose to work together, and our defence of the importance of connecting knowledge across disciplines [here]().

Let's start with the printed book that inspired this project: *The Feminine Monarchie: Or The Historie of Bees*, a seventeenth-century manual for beekeepers revised and reprinted three times (1609, 1623, 1634). This book was created by Charles Butler (1571-1647) with his printers, first Joseph Barnes, and then John Haviland. Butler was an Oxford graduate, a vicar, a teacher of grammar and rhetoric, a musician, and an apiarist. His book is full of practical information for beekeepers, and to help organise our reading experience he devised an innovative system of navigational devices. The most obvious navigational device he uses is the traditional Table of Contents (or 'Index of Chapters' as he calls it), which provides an overview of the information in the book in the order in which it appears. Butler's table is at the front of the book.[^1] However, this is only one device he uses. This table is immediately followed by another one, this time titled 'The Notes or the Contents' for each chapter. The term 'Notes' refers to and creates a list of the headings of sections within chapters, each one of which is given a number. Then there is another innovation that Butler introduces, creating pathways for the reader to explore throughout the book. Cross-references rely on a simple code, which Butler explains in the ['Preface to the Reader']({base}/literature/transcription#preface) thus: 'V. signifieth vide, or See, C. with his number the Chapter, and N. with his number the Marginall Note'. If the cross-reference omits the letter 'C.' then the reader should presume that it refers to 'some Note of the same Chapter' that they are reading. ([sig. ¶4v]({base}/literature/transcription#frontpar8))

Take just one of the many topics dealt with in this book: the impact of a rainy spring on early swarms. You can find this topic listed for Chapter 5 in the Index of Chapters. The Index will help you to find the passage in the chapter, which explains how a wet spring causes early swarms: 'A warme, calme, and showring spring causeth many and rathe swarmes, though sudden stormes doe hinder them. v.'. The letter v, in the text, highlighted in the image below, alerts us to a cross-reference in the margin: V.c. 7.n. 60. If we were to 'see' (v. or vide), i.e. turn to and look at Chapter 7 (c. 7), and then locate the note (n.) numbered 60 in the margin, where we discover that wet springs are also dangerous for early swarms.

There are hundreds and hundreds of cross-references like this throughout Butler's book. You may want to read this book in a linear way, from start to finish, and can do so easily by ignoring the cross-references; but you can also read this book in a connected way, following the links that Butler has provided, moving back and forth to build knowledge of a topic (like wet springs). In our born-digital edition of the 1623 edition (our copy text for our edition), these references appear as hyperlinks, so you can zigzag ([bee-like!](https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2022/12/honeybees-windy-conditions)) quickly through the text with a click rather than by turning pages. This system, in print or digital form, makes it easy for a beekeeper/ interested reader to locate what he or she wants to know quickly. It also reveals Butler's conception of the book as a store of interconnected knowledge.

This elaborate system of cross-referencing isn't the only print feature of Butler's book that is unusual. As we explain in an essay on [The Book as a Hive]({base}/literature/book-hive), Butler is sharing not just practical knowledge but an experience. He wants to take us *into* a hive. Several print features of 1623 and 1634, including the frontispiece of a hive, and perhaps also the floral and cell-like decorative features, as well as, crucially, the bee-song in a [sociable table-book format for four voices]({base}/music/music-book-layout) in [Chapter 5]({base}/literature/transcription#ch5), first introduced in 1623, as well as the phonetic spelling of the 1634 edition, indicate that Buter wanted to share his experience of getting inside a hive to understand bee behaviour, and bee emotions. Butler sees the hive as an acoustic space, and he uses his training as a musician and rhetorician listening for pitch and tone to understand what emotions the virgin queens are communicating at a crucial stage in the life of a colony: swarming. His book recreates this acoustic space so that musically-literate readers can 'pipe' – or imagine they are piping – like a virgin-queen to understand what is happening.

In our digital edition, you don't need to 'pipe' like a bee (unless you want to) to share this experience. You can listen instead to the performance of this song by [Ensemble Pro Victoria]({base}/music/EPV-performance), where the piping is represented with a wind instrument, or to another performance by [St Mary's Choir](), Cambridge, directed by Simon Jackson, where the piping is represented with the human voice, and/or listen to and watch Simon's student choristers at Peterhouse, Cambridge, [making sense of the bee song in rehearsal](). You might also want to read [Chapter 5]({base}/literature/transcription#ch5) in our born-digital edition, with the editorial notes turned 'on', to find out what the *Bee-ing Human* team – literary scholars, musicologists and scientists – have to say about this song and Butler's interpretation of piping bees in our collaborative annotation of this chapter.

<ImgContainer imgUrl="/assets/articles/introduction/editorial-notes-on.png" altText="A screenshot of the transcription highlighting the editorial notes option" caption="The editorial notes option turned on"/>

Butler created an acoustic hive over three editions. Our editing project is also interested in the evolution of this book, and the evolution of Butler's thinking, as he sought to share his lively experience in the field in print. In the age of the handpress, this involved a process that involves locking down words. It seems inimical to Butler's kind of thinking. And yet this technology, in the west invented famously by Gutenberg c.1440, was still quite young in the early seventeenth century.

Much like Butler took advantage of its print medium to create an interconnected active text, in designing the Digital Bee Book we took advantage of the inherent interconnectedness of the world wide web to present our multifaceted work as a series of connected articles, experiences, and datasets. Taking inspiration partly from Butler's obsessively cross-referenced text, partly from the common understanding of a bee hive, and partly from our many discussions around how to work together, we conceived of our project as a series of differing perspectives into a common space: which translated as four separate entries ([literature]({base}/literature), [music]({base}/music), [science]({base}/science), and [connections]({base}/connections)) into our Digital Bee Book, each offering a differing perspective on the shared objects and themes, at the same time that readers are allowed (and encouraged) to jump from perspective to perspective — from music to science, say — almost unnoticeably, by following one of the many cross-references in the articles, of simply by using the view selector on the top of the screen.

<ImgContainer imgUrl="/assets/articles/introduction/view-selector.png" altText="A screenshot of the header of the website with the view selector highlighted" caption="Changing perspectives"/>

It was very important to us that the design of the Digital Bee Book reflected as much as possible our understanding of how we worked together, and that that understanding would be communicated as simply as possible, in an easy to navigate environment that was simultaneaously familiar and new. [The landing page]({base}/) in particular, [as we explain elsewhere](), takes inspiration from both an abstracted beehive and the frontispiece to Butler's book; each of those cells representing either a honey storage cell (linking directly to an article inside the book), or an entryway into one of our four perspectives. It is also a visual representation of how we organise and relate our research during the project: we saw ourselves as working together in a beehive, with different roles contributing to a common goal.


[^1]: 'Table of Contents' in Adam Smyth and Dennis Duncan, *Book Parts*, p. 67.
